text: You've confirmed exactly which credential was compromised and traced what it did. Now comes the part that's easy to get wrong under pressure: containing it without taking down everything else running in that account or subscription. This lesson is about scoping containment to the actual blast radius, not reaching for the biggest switch available.

The instinct under pressure is to disable the whole IAM user, lock the entire account, or disable the subscription. That does stop the attacker, but it also stops every legitimate workload running there, turning a contained incident into a self-inflicted outage. The real goal is shrinking the attacker's reach to as close to zero as possible while leaving everything else running — which means acting on exactly the identity or resource your investigation already pointed to, and capturing evidence before you clean anything up.

In AWS, deactivate the specific leaked access key rather than the whole user — that stops it from being used again without touching any other key that user legitimately needs. But deactivation alone isn't enough, because it doesn't retroactively kill temporary STS sessions already issued from that key. AWS's own incident-response guidance documents a fix: an explicit-deny policy conditioned on the token's issue time. Because explicit denies always win, it invalidates every session older than your detection timestamp, without touching anything issued after you've rotated.

Azure's scoped equivalents work the same way. Block sign-in for one specific user or service principal with a targeted Conditional Access policy, rather than disabling the whole tenant. Revoke that identity's refresh tokens directly, since disabling the account alone doesn't invalidate sessions already issued. And if the compromise involved a secret added to an app registration, remove just that secret — deleting the whole app registration can break every legitimate workload still depending on it.

The same logic applies to compromised compute. Isolate a suspect EC2 instance by swapping it to a security group with no rules at all, and snapshot the EBS volume before touching anything else — terminating it destroys the forensic evidence you need. Azure offers an equivalent isolate action in Defender for Cloud, or the same NSG-swap, followed by a disk snapshot. When the real problem is one over-privileged role assignment, remove that one assignment instead of a blanket deny at the subscription root.

That completes the chapter's arc: a leaked credential gets enumerated, escalated, and persisted; CloudTrail and the Azure logs prove exactly what happened; and containment shuts down precisely the identity or resource responsible, evidence preserved, nothing else disrupted. The capstone labs ahead put this sequence into practice against a simulated compromise.
